families.s: HSE introduction to human factors in health and safety
families.t: task design, individual capability, organisation, work environment, competence, culture and safety management
f: Human factors include environmental, organisational and job factors together with human and individual characteristics that influence behaviour and safety.
Human factors considers what people are asked to do, who is doing it and the organisation in which the work takes place.
Job, individual and organisational factors are interrelated and should not be assessed in isolation.
Task design should account for human strengths and limitations, including perception, attention and decision making.
People differ in physical capability, vision, hearing, dexterity, knowledge, experience and other characteristics relevant to work.
Workplace design, equipment, information and the environment should support rather than hinder safe task performance.
Organisational factors such as work patterns, culture, resources, communications and leadership influence behaviour.
Human factors should be included within the safety management system like other risk-control systems.
families.g: Task design, individual capability, organisation, work environment, competence, culture and safety management guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE proactive management of human failures
families.t: human error, violations, performance-influencing factors, risk assessment, error tolerance and workforce involvement
f: Everyone can make errors regardless of training or motivation, and workplace consequences can be severe.
Human failure contributes to many accidents, incidents and hazardous-substance exposures.
Human failure should be managed as robustly as technical and engineering safety measures.
Risk assessment should identify significant potential human errors in safety-critical tasks.
Assessment should identify performance-influencing factors such as poor design, distraction, time pressure, workload, competence and communication.
Controls should preferably redesign tasks or equipment and make systems more tolerant of error.
Human failures include unintended errors and deliberate deviations or violations.
Incident investigations should explain why people failed rather than stop at the label 'operator error'.
families.g: Human error, violations, performance-influencing factors, risk assessment, error tolerance and workforce involvement guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE identification and control of human-error types
families.t: slips, lapses, mistakes, violations, omissions, commissions, error-tolerant design and structured assessment
f: Human-factors work aims to optimise human performance and reduce human failures.
HSE points to a structured seven-step approach for identifying and managing human failures.
Slips and lapses are unintended actions or omissions during familiar tasks.
Mistakes occur when the intended action or decision is wrong, often in new or poorly understood situations.
Violations are deliberate deviations from rules or procedures and are usually not malicious.
Training alone cannot eliminate slips and lapses, so design should reduce likelihood and consequences.
Rules and procedures should be relevant, practical and explained so that violation causes can be addressed.
Assessments should consider both errors of omission and errors of commission.
families.g: Slips, lapses, mistakes, violations, omissions, commissions, error-tolerant design and structured assessment guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE human factors in accident and near-miss investigations
families.t: underlying causes, latent conditions, performance-influencing factors, trained investigators, recommendations and organisational learning
f: Accident investigations should consider why human failures occurred.
Finding underlying, latent or root causes is central to preventing recurrence.
Investigations should not stop after identifying an operator action or decision.
Investigators should identify the performance-influencing factors that made an error more likely.
Task design, procedures, workload, competence, supervision, communication and organisational conditions may need examination.
Near misses, incidents and accidents should be thoroughly investigated by people trained in investigation techniques.
Lessons from investigations should be communicated widely and recommendations implemented promptly.
Repeated failure to implement earlier recommendations indicates weak organisational learning.
families.g: Underlying causes, latent conditions, performance-influencing factors, trained investigators, recommendations and organisational learning guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.

families.s: HSE assessment of safety-critical staffing levels
families.t: staff numbers, skills, location, timing, organisational change, emergency coverage, workload and competence
f: Suitable staffing means having the right numbers of the right people in the right place at the right time.
Staffing changes often accompany downsizing, delayering or multi-skilling.
Staffing arrangements should be assessed before and after organisational change.
Staffing level is closely related to workload and the availability of skilled personnel.
Organisational changes to roles, departments, contractors or staff numbers can affect hazard control.
Peak workload, incidents, turnarounds and abnormal operations can require additional capability.
Competence assurance should cover all people performing safety-related work, including managers.
Assessments should consider normal operation, maintenance, emergencies, absences and the ability to supervise work.
families.g: Staff numbers, skills, location, timing, organisational change, emergency coverage, workload and competence guidance is general organisational and human-factors evidence and does not prove current staffing, competence, behaviour, controls, performance or exact risk at an individual parcel.
